results.summary: CODES trial: CBT specifically designed for PNES did not significantly reduce seizure frequency compared to standard medical care at 12 months, but did improve secondary outcomes including psychological distress, psychosocial functioning, and quality of life.
results.title: Cognitive behavioral therapy for functional neurological disorder: A randomized controlled trial

results.summary: Expert consensus recommends: (1) diagnosis using positive clinical signs (Hoover sign, tremor entrainment), not by exclusion; (2) clear and empathetic communication of the diagnosis; (3) multidisciplinary treatment including physiotherapy, psychology/psychiatry, and occupational therapy; (4) avoidance of unnecessary investigations that reinforce illness behavior.
results.title: Consensus recommendations for the diagnosis and treatment of functional neurological disorder

results.summary: Systematic review supporting the role of specialized physical therapy for functional motor disorder. FND-informed physiotherapy focuses on movement retraining, distraction techniques, and graded activity rather than strengthening exercises.
results.title: Physical rehabilitation for functional motor symptoms: a systematic review

output.summary: Functional neurological disorder is characterized by positive clinical signs of internal inconsistency. Multidisciplinary management — physiotherapy adapted for functional motor symptoms, CBT for non-epileptic attacks, and treatment of comorbid psychiatric disorders — is the evidence-based approach. Prognosis is associated with younger age, shorter symptom duration, absence of comorbid personality disorder, and engagement with psychological treatment in published cohorts.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not pursue ever-expanding negative investigations — per Stone 2018, repeated negative workups reinforce illness conviction and worsen prognosis
Do not frame the diagnosis as 'all in your head', 'nothing wrong', or 'we couldn't find anything' — this damages the therapeutic alliance and is the most common avoidable harm in FND
Do not perform invasive testing (lumbar puncture, nerve biopsy, muscle biopsy, cerebral angiography) when positive rule-in signs are present and there is no clinical indication
Do not order EMG/NCS, muscle biopsy, or nerve biopsy as part of an FND workup — these invasive tests reinforce the somatic illness model per Stone 2018
Do not start or continue long-term anti-epileptic drugs for functional (psychogenic non-epileptic) seizures — AEDs are ineffective for PNES and expose the patient to side effects
Do not give benzodiazepines as abortive therapy for witnessed PNES events (no benefit and risk of respiratory depression)
Do not give gadolinium without a specific indication — contrast adds cost and risk and answers no question that positive functional signs have not already answered

Do not repeat the brain MRI, the laboratory panel or the lumbar puncture once a first normal study and positive rule-in signs are documented: each repetition strengthens the patient's belief that something organic has been missed
required_recommendations: Do NOT make the diagnosis by exclusion: document at least one positive rule-in sign, which is the act that establishes it
Obtain video-EEG capturing a habitual event with normal interictal EEG to confirm PNES
Communicate the diagnosis transparently using positive language and the rule-in signs as the basis
Refer for FND-informed physiotherapy and CBT / psychological therapy
Order a comprehensive neuropsychological battery to characterize comorbid depression, anxiety, somatization, and trauma exposure — informs treatment planning (criteria-pack 'recommended' tier)

Communicate the diagnosis transparently using positive language anchored on the rule-in signs; explicitly state the diagnosis is FND, the symptoms are real and involuntary, and there is an evidence-based treatment plan
Refer to specialized FND-informed physiotherapy (for functional motor symptoms) and to CBT / psychological therapy (for PNES and comorbid mood / anxiety)

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG has no diagnostic role in FND; cardiac etiology is not on the differential for the presenting neurological deficit.
Echocardiography has no role in FND; no structural cardiac question is raised by the presentation.
Cardiac rhythm monitoring is not indicated; the events are non-syncopal and the rule-in signs point to FND.
Non-contrast head CT adds no information beyond MRI for an FND workup and contributes diagnostic noise plus radiation exposure.
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in typical FND; invasive testing reinforces somatic illness model and adds iatrogenic risk without changing management.
Advanced PET imaging has no indication in FND; standard MRI is the appropriate structural workup.

Nerve conduction studies and EMG have no role once positive functional signs are documented: the deficit is not neuromuscular, the study is uncomfortable, and a normal result reinforces the patient's search for an organic cause — the principal iatrogenic harm in this condition
Somatosensory evoked potentials answer a question about a lesion in the somatosensory pathway; a midline-splitting, non-anatomical sensory deficit is not that question

accepted: Functional neurological disorder (conversion disorder) with weakness and psychogenic non-epileptic seizures

differential.key_features: Witnessed convulsive-appearing events; ictal video-EEG showing absence of electrographic correlate during a captured habitual event is the key differentiator.
Sensorimotor symptoms in a young adult raise demyelinating disease; brain (and when indicated spine) MRI without T2/FLAIR lesions or enhancement argues against an active demyelinating process.
Sudden focal deficit raises stroke; non-anatomical weakness pattern with positive Hoover sign, normal MRI/DWI, and intact reflexes argue against vascular etiology.
Focal complaints warrant imaging; normal brain MRI without lesion, mass, or enhancement effectively excludes a structural cause for the presenting deficit.
Non-dermatomal sensory loss, normal reflexes, and (when obtained) normal EMG/NCS argue against peripheral nerve or root pathology.
Episodic neurological symptoms can occur in autoimmune encephalitis; normal MRI, normal EEG background, and (when obtained) negative antibody panel render this very unlikely.

key_clinical_evidence: FND is a positive diagnosis based on rule-in signs (Hoover, tremor entrainment, give-way weakness, non-dermatomal sensory loss with midline split) — not a diagnosis of exclusion (Espay 2018, Stone 2018).

Brain MRI and basic laboratory testing are OPTIONAL here, not due diligence: the diagnosis rests on the positive signs, and each additional negative study is a cost and an iatrogenic harm rather than a confirmation. Where imaging is recommended in this case it is for one specific alternative question, once.
Over-investigation is the principal iatrogenic harm in FND; every additional negative test reinforces the patient's illness conviction and worsens prognosis (Stone 2018).
Psychiatric comorbidity (anxiety, depression, trauma) is common and informs treatment planning but is NOT required for the diagnosis and does not 'explain' the symptoms in a reductive sense.
Diagnostic communication matters: using positive language anchored on the rule-in signs is associated with better engagement and outcomes (Stone 2018).
Evidence-based treatment is multidisciplinary — CBT for PNES and FND-informed physiotherapy for functional motor symptoms (Nielsen 2015).
Video-EEG capturing a habitual event with normal interictal EEG is diagnostic for PNES (ILAE PNES Task Force 2013); routine EEG alone is insufficient.

Interim composition decision, August 2026: FND remains only to keep the frozen dataset at 20 conditions/600 cases. The positive functional-neurological examination is the sole required diagnostic act; every instrumental test is optional and case-targeted. DLB remains the preferred future replacement when composition work resumes.

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive functional signs elicited and documented: Collapsing (give-way) weakness, Hoover sign, Midline-splitting sensory loss, Non-anatomical sensory loss, Internal inconsistency on repeat testing, Dragging monoplegic gait, Improvement with attentional distraction, Forced eye closure with resistance to passive opening, Tremor entrainment test. Functional neurological disorder is a rule-in diagnosis under DSM-5 and the criterion satisfied here is clinical incompatibility, not the absence of another disease. No further investigation is required to make the diagnosis; whatever imaging or laboratory testing is performed is for a separate, specific question.

clinical_pearls: FND is the second most common reason for outpatient neurology consultation and should be diagnosed by positive signs, not by exclusion
The Hoover sign has high sensitivity and specificity for functional leg weakness and should be tested in all patients presenting with lower extremity weakness
Psychogenic non-epileptic seizures account for approximately 20-30% of patients referred to epilepsy monitoring units
Early diagnosis and appropriate communication of the diagnosis are the most important prognostic factors in FND
Psychiatric comorbidity (especially depression, anxiety, PTSD, and history of childhood trauma) is common but not universal in FND; absence of psychiatric history does not exclude the diagnosis

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Miguel Santos is a 22-year-old right-handed man who presents to the neurology service as a direct admission from his primary care physician's office for evaluation of progressive right leg weakness and recurrent episodes of whole-body shaking over the past six weeks. The patient reports that approximately eight weeks ago he witnessed a severe motor vehicle accident in which a pedestrian was struck and killed. He was deeply affected by this event and has since experienced nightmares, flashbacks, and heightened anxiety. Two weeks after the accident, he noticed that his right leg began to feel 'heavy and weak,' initially intermittent but progressively worsening to the point where he now requires a wheelchair for mobility. He describes the weakness as affecting his entire right leg from the hip downward, and he also notes decreased sensation over the right leg and right lower abdomen. He denies any back pain, bowel or bladder dysfunction, or left-sided symptoms. Concurrently, he has developed episodes of shaking involving his arms and sometimes his whole body, occurring two to four times daily, each lasting 30 seconds to 3 minutes. During these episodes he reports being aware of his surroundings but unable to control the movements. He denies tongue biting, urinary incontinence, or post-event confusion. His boyfriend has witnessed multiple episodes and describes them as variable in intensity and pattern, noting that they sometimes occur during stressful conversations. He reports that he has never injured himself during an episode and that he can respond to questions throughout. He was seen in an outside emergency department three weeks ago where a CT head was unremarkable and he was discharged with a referral to neurology. His primary care physician, noting the progressive nature and functional impairment, arranged for direct inpatient admission for comprehensive evaluation. The patient is worried that he may have multiple sclerosis or epilepsy and is seeking answers. He acknowledges significant psychological distress since the accident but does not believe his symptoms are related to stress.

neurological_exam.additional: During the examination, two brief episodes of bilateral upper extremity shaking lasting approximately 45 seconds and 30 seconds were witnessed. During these events, the patient's eyes were tightly closed (forced eye closure with resistance to passive opening), he demonstrated asynchronous, irregular, side-to-side head movements, and the tremor was variable in frequency (2-6 Hz) and amplitude. The tremor entrained to examiner-imposed rhythm during contralateral hand tapping. He remained responsive to verbal commands throughout, stating 'I can't stop it.' No post-event confusion.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin testing performed normally on the left; on the right, patient demonstrates inconsistent performance with exaggerated swaying but no true dysmetria. Rapid alternating movements intact bilaterally.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II: Visual fields full to confrontation bilaterally. Pupils equal, round, reactive to light 3mm to 2mm bilaterally. Fundoscopic exam unremarkable, no papilledema. CN III/IV/VI: Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus. CN V: Sensation intact to light touch in all three divisions bilaterally. CN VII: Face symmetric at rest and with activation. CN VIII: Hearing grossly intact to finger rub bilaterally. CN IX/X: Palate elevates symmetrically. CN XI: Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. CN XII: Tongue midline, no atrophy or fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Patient uses a wheelchair and states he cannot walk due to right leg weakness. When assisted to stand, demonstrates a dragging gait pattern with the right leg held stiffly behind. However, on observational testing when distracted, he was noted to bear full weight on the right leg momentarily while adjusting his hospital gown. No Trendelenburg sign. Romberg testing: dramatic swaying in all directions without falling, with self-correction at extreme sway angles (functional Romberg).
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Glasgow Coma Scale 15. Speech fluent, normal rate and prosody. Affect is anxious with intermittent tearfulness when discussing symptoms. Attention intact, able to recite months of the year backward. Memory 3/3 registration, 3/3 recall at 5 minutes. No evidence of cognitive impairment.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone normal in bilateral upper extremities. Right lower extremity demonstrates give-way weakness: initial resistance followed by sudden collapse of effort in hip flexion (2/5 on initial testing, 5/5 when distracted during seated hip flexion while donning shoes). Left lower extremity strength 5/5 throughout. Upper extremities 5/5 bilaterally. Hoover sign positive on the right: involuntary hip extension strength is full when testing left hip flexion against resistance, but voluntary right hip flexion is reportedly 2/5. No pronator drift. No muscle atrophy or fasciculations.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor (downgoing) bilaterally. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reports decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick over the entire right leg extending to the exact midline of the groin and abdomen, with a sharp demarcation at midline. This non-anatomical pattern does not follow any dermatomal or peripheral nerve distribution. Vibration sense intact at bilateral great toes, medial malleoli, and tibial tuberosities. Proprioception intact in all digits. Upper extremity sensation intact throughout.
